endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions: Lifecycle Management and Marketing Submission Recommendations (draft guidance)
endorsements.quote: Furthermore, information gaps may lead to overreliance on the device 2239 output for follow-up.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Some notable end-user tendencies that could alter model effectiveness and performance and should be evaluated include: • Ambiguity/uncertainty aversion can lead to lack of use or improper use.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology

endorsements.title: FUTURE-AI: international consensus guideline for trustworthy and deployable artificial intelligence in healthcare
endorsements.quote: The usability tests should gather evidence on the user’s satisfaction, performance and productivity, and assess human factors that might affect the usage of the AI tool57 (eg, confidence, learnability, automation bias).

endorsements.title: Developing, purchasing, implementing and monitoring AI tools in radiology: practical considerations. A multi-society statement
endorsements.issuer: ACR, CAR, ESR, RANZCR, RSNA; Radiol Artif Intell 2024 (PMID 38251899, doi:10.1148/ryai.230513)
endorsements.quote: How do users need to be trained and which psychological effects need to be considered with regard to human-AI-interaction?

endorsements.title: Considerations for the regulation of generative AI-enabled medical devices (discussion paper)
endorsements.quote: the avoidance of coercive, emotionally manipulative, or otherwise inappropriate or abusive language;

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: (4) Transparency: Can end users appropriately use, trust, or distrust outputs?

endorsements.title: From prediction to intervention: causal digital twins for personalized clinical decision support
endorsements.quote: Ultimately, maintaining human oversight and emphasizing interpretability are essential to ensure that causal digital twins enhance, rather than replace, clinical judgment [ 23 ].

endorsements.title: A six-level clinical autonomy framework for artificial intelligence in dentistry
endorsements.quote: Beyond diagnostic accuracy, evaluation should incorporate human–AI interaction metrics, including decision latency, trust calibration, and susceptibility to automation bias.

endorsements.title: A testable framework linking diagnostic AI contribution to outcome measurement in clinical decision support
endorsements.quote: When AI-CDSS presents a top-ranked suggestion, differential diagnosis, or risk score, evaluation should consider anchoring and automation bias.

endorsements.title: A Human-Governed Clinical Informatics Framework for Safe AI-Assisted Mental Health Counseling: Secondary Framework Development and Requirement Mapping Study
endorsements.quote: Staff should be trained to recognize automation bias and apply the high-risk checklist consistently.

endorsements.title: The Long road to AI-physician partnership starts with learners: a map for AI in medical education
endorsements.quote: Education is one layer among others, such as subpopulation testing before deployment and naming accountability for who owns the output of the AI model.

evidence.title: Evaluating the Human Safety Net: Observational study of Physician Responses to Unsafe AI Recommendations in high-fidelity Simulation
evidence.outcome: Whether intensivists detect and reject unsafe AI treatment recommendations in simulation
evidence.effect: Most clinicians promptly rejected unsafe AI recommendations, with many seeking senior assistance; a few accepted unsafe recommendations after nurse influence.
evidence.quote: Most clinicians promptly rejected unsafe AI recommendations, with many seeking senior assistance.

evidence.title: Digital Pathology with AI for Cervical Biopsies: Diagnostic Accuracy at the CIN2+ Threshold
evidence.outcome: Expert detection of incorrect AI outputs
evidence.effect: After adjudication, ACIS increased from EE-alone 13/20 to 18/20, and false invasive SCC calls decreased to 1/20.
evidence.quote: After expert adjudication in the EE + P2 condition, ACIS was restored to 18/20 and false invasive calls were largely removed (SCC 1/20).

evidence.title: Quantifying the impact of a computer-aided diagnostic score on the clinical diagnosis of functional seizures
evidence.outcome: Whether users detect incorrect AI outputs; rates of being persuaded or misled by FSLS
evidence.effect: Group 2 was never misled; Group 5 improved 21% from persuasion and lost 4% from being misled; readers persuaded in only 30%-45% of cases when FSLS was correct.
evidence.quote: The accuracy of the near highest performance group (Group 2) improved because they were persuaded by the FSLS, but they were never misled (Figures 4 and S4–S6).

evidence.title: Human-in-the-Loop Enhances Machine Learning Inference in Intraoperative Optical Coherence Tomography Glioma Imaging
evidence.outcome: Whether clinicians detect incorrect AI outputs rather than passively accepting them
evidence.effect: Surgeons rejected 9 of 13 (69%) AI false-positive cases; HITL accuracy exceeded SVM baseline, indicating no blind adherence. Limitation: 4 of 13 errors were still confirmed.
evidence.quote: Relying on their domain knowledge of tissue topology, the surgeon rejects the AI’s suggestion in 9 of these cases and overrides the machine.
evidence.sample_unit: intraoperative OCT scans (27 patients; 5 neurosurgeon raters)

evidence.title: An LLM chatbot to facilitate primary-to-specialist care transitions: a randomized controlled trial
evidence.outcome: Direct adoption of LLM content in physician clinical notes (automation bias)
evidence.effect: Classifier distinguishing PreA-assisted vs No-PreA notes near random (F1 0.57; P = 0.81; ΔF1 < 0.02); no domain differences (P = 0.10–0.90).
evidence.quote: Classification analysis yielded near-random discriminability (F1 score 0.57; P = 0.81; ΔF1 < 0.02).

evidence.title: Encounter Appropriateness Score for You Model: Development and Pilot Implementation of a Predictive Model to Identify Visits Appropriate for Telehealth in Rheumatology
evidence.outcome: Whether providers distinguished true model recommendations from artificial (false) recommendations in pilot
evidence.effect: Providers agreed more with true than artificial recommendations (Cohen's κ = 0.45, P < 0.001); moderate discrimination; 201 pilot encounters; model increased appropriate telehealth visits.
evidence.quote: Providers were more likely to agree with true versus artificial recommendations (Cohen's κ = 0.45, P < 0.001), and the model increased the number of appropriate telehealth visits.

evidence.title: Patient and dermatologists' perspectives on augmented intelligence for melanoma screening: A prospective study
evidence.venue: Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology : JEADV
evidence.outcome: Dermatologist overreliance on benign CNN classification in divergent risk assessments
evidence.effect: Only 1.5% (n = 3/205) of dermatologists trusted a benign CNN classification over their own malignancy suspicion, despite 90.2%-96.1% reporting high trust in AI results.
evidence.quote: Contrarily, in divergent risk assessments, only 1.5% of dermatologists trusted a benign CNN-classification more than personal malignancy suspicion (n = 3/205).

evidence.title: Real-World Diagnostic Performance and Clinical Utility of Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Interpretation for Detection of Lung Metastasis on CT in Patients With Colorectal Cancer
evidence.outcome: Radiologist acceptance of AI false-positive detections (automation bias)
evidence.effect: Stand-alone AI had 381 false-positive detections in 634 patients without metastasis; only one AI false positive was reported as positive by radiologists.
evidence.quote: Stand-alone AI correctly detected metastasis in 24 of 29 patients but had 381 false-positive detections in 634 patients without metastasis; only one AI false-positive was reported as positive by interpretating radiologists.

evidence.title: Human factors in the clinical implementation of deep learning-based automated contouring of pelvic organs at risk for MRI-guided radiotherapy
evidence.outcome: Presence of automation bias and its dosimetric consequence in planners using AI contours
evidence.effect: Automation bias was observed in planners. Only 4 deviating slices in 2 patients were graded low clinical significance, none moderate or high. Dose differences were not significant.
evidence.quote: Automation bias was observed, but it had little deleterious effect on treatment planning.

evidence.title: Early Experiences of Integrating an Artificial Intelligence-Based Diagnostic Decision Support System into Radiology Settings: A Qualitative Study
evidence.venue: Studies in health technology and informatics
evidence.outcome: Differences between expert and novice users in critically evaluating AI recommendations
evidence.effect: Experts critically evaluated system recommendations and compensated for system limitations to achieve more reliable performance; novice users differed in patterns of use. No quantitative error-detection rates reported.
evidence.quote: There were differences in patterns of use between experts and novice users with experts critically evaluating system recommendations and actively compensating for system limitations to achieve more reliable performance.

evidence.title: Experience of Implementing Deep Learning-Based Automatic Contouring in Breast Radiation Therapy Planning: Insights From Over 2000 Cases
evidence.venue: International journal of radiation oncology, biology, physics
evidence.outcome: Reliance on auto-contours and automation bias risk after system implementation
evidence.effect: Adoption was associated with increased reliance on automated settings (higher DSC and lower HD95 between auto and final contours postimplementation for several OARs and targets), indicating potential automation bias.
evidence.quote: In our study, the adoption of an auto-contouring system was associated with an increased reliance on automated settings, underscoring its utility and the potential risk of automation bias.

evidence.title: Chinese Oncologists' Perspectives on Integrating AI into Clinical Practice: Cross-Sectional Survey Study
evidence.outcome: Oncologists' concern about overreliance on AI
evidence.effect: 162/228 (71%) of oncologists were concerned about overreliance on AI; 163/228 (71.5%) worried AI could mislead diagnosis and treatment.
evidence.quote: The study revealed that the most prominent concerns were the potential for AI to mislead diagnosis and treatment (163/228, 71.5%); an overreliance on AI (162/228, 71%); data and algorithm bias (123/228, 54%); issues with data security and patient privacy (123/228, 54%); and a lag in the adaptation of laws, regulations, and policies in keeping up with AI's development (115/228, 50.4%).

evidence.title: Assessing the Utility, Impact, and Adoption Challenges of an Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Prescription Advisory Tool for Type 2 Diabetes Management: Qualitative Study
evidence.outcome: Clinician-reported concerns about overreliance and automation bias with AI prescription advisory
evidence.effect: Concerns about overreliance and automation bias were raised by clinicians and hindered adoption; not measured directly.
evidence.quote: However, the interpretability of the risk scores, concerns about overreliance and automation bias, and issues surrounding accountability and liability hindered the adoption of the APA tool in clinical practice.

evidence.title: Public risk perception, institutional AI adoption, and diagnostic safety: An exploratory cross-level analysis using a tracer condition approach
evidence.outcome: Association between hospital AI usage intensity and misdiagnosis rate for acute imaging-dependent tracer condition
evidence.effect: Higher AI usage intensity was positively associated with misdiagnosis rates (β = 0.28, p < 0.001), suggesting automation bias in time-sensitive acute triage; attenuated by high public trust and remoteness.
evidence.quote: Within the specific context of the tracer condition, higher AI usage intensity was positively associated with misdiagnosis rates (β = 0.28, p < 0.001), suggesting a pattern of "automation bias" in time-sensitive acute triage.

evidence.title: Radiologist Perceptions of an AI Tool for Intracranial Hemorrhage Detection in Teleradiology: Cross-Sectional Survey Study
evidence.outcome: Self-reported reduced scrutiny after AI-negative result and conditional trust in AI output
evidence.effect: Reduced scrutiny after AI-negative result reported by 4/65 (6.2%; 95% CI 2.4%-14.8%); 50.8% trusted AI when it agreed with their read vs 3.1% when it conflicted.
evidence.quote: Self-reported reduced scrutiny after an AI-negative result was uncommon (4/65, 6.2%; 95% CI 2.4%-14.8%).

evidence.title: Frontline Health Workers' Perspectives of the World Health Organization Skin Neglected Tropical Diseases App in Kenya: Qualitative Study on AI-Embedded mHealth Implementation
evidence.outcome: FHW reliance on or deferral to AI diagnostic output
evidence.effect: Most FHWs used the app as an assistive tool, but a minority reported diagnostic deferral to the AI output, raising clinical autonomy concerns.
evidence.quote: While most FHWs used the app in line with its intended role as an assistive tool, a minority reported situations of diagnostic deferral to the AI output, highlighting potential considerations of clinical autonomy.

evidence.title: Human-AI Co-reasoning for Clinical Diagnosis with Evidence-Integrated Language Agent
evidence.outcome: Automation bias when physicians use AI assistance in diagnosis
evidence.effect: Collaborative use introduced risks of automation bias, despite helping correct initial errors.
evidence.quote: When used collaboratively, PULSE enabled physicians to correct initial errors and broaden diagnostic hypotheses, but also introduced risks of automation bias.

evidence.title: What Users Cannot See: Evaluating LLM Emotional Support Beyond User Preference
evidence.outcome: lay detection of problematic endorsement
evidence.effect: Lay raters detected only 60% of expert-confirmed Endorse instances and rated personas similarly helpful and desirable.
evidence.quote: Two independent LLM judges substantially agreed with clinically trained raters, yet lay raters detected only 60% of expert-confirmed Endorse instances and rated the personas similarly helpful and desirable.

evidence.title: Not All Uncertainty Is Equal: How Uncertainty Granularity Shapes Human Verification in LLM-Assisted Decision Making
evidence.outcome: external verification
evidence.effect: No effect sizes reported; relation-level uncertainty reduced internet searches and URL checking, shifting users toward LLM reliance.
evidence.quote: Notably, relation-level uncertainty also reduced external verification (i.e., internet searches, checking provided URLs), steering users away from independent fact-checking and toward reliance on the LLM and its accompanying uncertainty cues.

evidence.title: Large language models improve physician accuracy but lead to false reliance
evidence.outcome: Physician resistance to incorrect LLM answers when citation-supported
evidence.effect: When an incorrect LLM answer appeared citation-supported, physician resistance fell from 92% to 34.8%; adoption of correct advice rose from 34% to 76.9%.
evidence.quote: perceived support increased adoption of correct advice from 34% to 76.9% but when an incorrect LLM answer appeared citation-supported, physician resistance to it fell from 92% to 34.8%.

evidence.title: Characterizing Rhetorical Misalignment in Decision-Making with Language Models
evidence.outcome: Rate of harmful decision flips from correct to incorrect after LLM-generated information
evidence.effect: LLMs induce an average 2.81% rate of harmful decision flips across different models, where clinician participants change from a correct to an incorrect answer.
evidence.quote: By measuring how LLM-generated information affects decisions, we observe that LLMs induce an average 2.81% rate of harmful decision flips across different models, where clinician participants change from a correct to an incorrect answer.

evidence.title: Automation Bias in Large Language Model Assisted Diagnostic Reasoning Among AI-Trained Physicians
evidence.outcome: Physician diagnostic accuracy after exposure to erroneous versus error-free LLM recommendations (automation bias)
evidence.effect: Mean accuracy 84.9% (error-free) vs 73.3% (flawed); adjusted difference -14.0 percentage points (95% CI -8.3 to -19.7; P<.0001). Top-choice accuracy difference -18.3 points.
evidence.quote: This trial demonstrates that erroneous LLM recommendations significantly degrade physicians’ diagnostic performance by inducing automation bias, even in AI-trained physicians.

evidence.title: Physician Facing AI Tools Show Distinct Failure Modes Under Structured Stress Testing
evidence.outcome: Susceptibility of AI to following clinically incorrect directives from the physician user
evidence.effect: ChatGPT for Clinicians followed clinically incorrect directives in 1.7% vs 8.0% for OpenEvidence (adjusted OR 0.07; 95% CI 0.02-0.21; P < .001).
evidence.quote: ChatGPT for Clinicians captured more gold-standard critical elements than OpenEvidence (81.4% ± 18.1% vs 61.0% ± 23.5%; adjusted difference, 20.3 percentage points; 95% CI, 18.3 to 22.4;  P < .001) and was less susceptible to clinically incorrect directives (1.7% vs 8.0%; adjusted odds ratio, 0.07; 95% CI, 0.02-0.21;  P < .001).
evidence.sample_unit: responses (to 1920 prompts across 60 simulated critical care vignettes)

evidence.title: Diagnostic Reasoning With and Without AI: Automation Bias in Pre-Clerkship Medical Students
evidence.outcome: Whether students detected when AI changed their diagnostic ranking for better or worse (automation bias)
evidence.effect: Accuracy improved in 65 students and worsened in 26 after AI use. Both groups rated AI as more influential than students whose accuracy did not change (P = .006 and P = .001).
evidence.quote: Students benefited most from AI when their baseline reasoning was weakest but could not reliably distinguish helpful from harmful AI influence, consistent with automation bias.

evidence.title: Pediatric Autism Diagnosis Accuracy and Confidence: A Comparison of Experienced and Inexperienced Clinicians Making Decisions with and without AI Decision Support
evidence.outcome: Whether clinicians detected incorrect AI suggestions; confidence when AI wrong
evidence.effect: Trainees showed 0% accuracy when ADIS was wrong vs 68.75% when correct; trained clinicians 66.67% and 56.25%; confidence high regardless of ADIS correctness.
evidence.quote: Despite these differences in accuracy, confidence was high regardless of ADIS correctness.

evidence.title: Explainable AI as a Double-Edged Sword in Dermatology: The Impact on Clinicians versus The Public
evidence.outcome: automation bias after incorrect AI
evidence.effect: AI suggestions first led to worse outcomes when the AI was incorrect for both groups.
evidence.quote: Presenting AI suggestions first also led to worse outcomes when the AI was incorrect for both groups.

evidence.title: Certified large language model-based diagnostic decision support in rheumatology: the ALLIANCE multicentre randomised controlled trial
evidence.outcome: Overconfidence and over-reliance on AI output among physicians
evidence.effect: Exploratory analyses showed persistent overconfidence and substantial AI over-reliance; no quantitative estimates given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Exploratory analyses showed persistent overconfidence and substantial AI over-reliance.

evidence.title: MDT-guided language-model reasoning for spinal infection diagnosis
evidence.outcome: correct-to-incorrect diagnostic transitions with AI advice
evidence.effect: There were 41 correct-to-incorrect transitions with fixed AI advice.
evidence.quote: In the reader study, five clinicians made 1,716 matched reader–case–decision assessments; accuracy was 92.1% with fixed AI advice and 89.1% without advice (difference, 3.03 percentage points; fixed-reader case-bootstrap 95% confidence interval, 1.47 to 4.55), with 93 incorrect-to-correct and 41 correct-to-incorrect transitions.

evidence.title: Evaluating the Human Safety Net: Observational study of Physician Responses to Unsafe AI Recommendations in high-fidelity Simulation
evidence.outcome: acceptance of unsafe AI recommendations
evidence.effect: A few physicians were influenced to accept unsafe AI recommendations.
evidence.quote: Additionally, we observed human-human interactions, where an experimenter played the role of a bedside nurse, influencing a few physicians to accept unsafe AI recommendations.

evidence.title: Integrating AI in Clinical Education: Evaluating General Practice Residents’ Proficiency in Distinguishing AI-Generated Hallucinations and Its Impacting Factors
evidence.outcome: Whether users detect incorrect AI outputs
evidence.effect: Residents had low error detection accuracy (55%) and low sensitivity (d' 0.39), indicating poor detection of incorrect AI outputs.
evidence.quote: The study concluded that residents struggled to identify AI errors, particularly in clinical cases, emphasizing the importance of improving AI literacy and critical thinking for effective integration into medical education.

evidence.title: Can incorrect artificial intelligence (AI) results impact radiologists, and if so, what can we do about it? A multi-reader pilot study of lung cancer detection with chest radiography
evidence.outcome: Radiologist overreliance on incorrect AI
evidence.effect: FNs rose from 2.7% to 20.7–33.0%; FPs from 51.4% to 80.5–86.0%.
evidence.quote: Relative to the No AI condition (FN = 2.7%, FP = 51.4%), FN and FPs were higher in the Keep AI (No Box) (FN = 33.0%, FP = 86.0%), Delete AI (No Box) (FN = 26.7%, FP = 80.5%), and Keep AI (Box) (FN = to 20.7%, FP = 80.5%) conditions (all ps < 0.05).
evidence.sample_unit: radiologists (each reading 90 chest radiographs across 4 conditions)

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence suppression as a strategy to mitigate artificial intelligence automation bias
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Proportion of clinician errors attributable to automation bias, across expertise levels
evidence.effect: Clinicians' errors in AI-assisted round associated with automation bias accounted for 45.5% of total mistakes; affected clinicians of all expertise levels.
evidence.quote: However, the clinicians' errors in the AI-assisted round were associated with automation bias, accounting for 45.5% of the total mistakes.
evidence.sample_unit: clinicians (each diagnosing 200 ACL MRIs with and without AI)

evidence.title: Discrepancy between perceptions and acceptance of clinical decision support Systems: implementation of artificial intelligence for vancomycin dosing
evidence.venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
evidence.outcome: Pharmacist acceptance of AI vancomycin dose recommendations after reveal (algorithm aversion)
evidence.effect: Pharmacists' empiric doses differed from the CDSS in 88/104 (85%) cases; after reveal, 69/88 (78%) remained discrepant and pharmacists would not alter their recommendations.
evidence.quote: In discrepant cases, pharmacists indicated they would not alter their recommendations.
evidence.sample_unit: critical care pharmacists (semi-structured interviews; 104 case discussions)

evidence.title: Reader bias in breast cancer screening related to cancer prevalence and artificial intelligence decision support-a reader study
evidence.outcome: Whether radiologists detect and resist incorrect AI outputs (automation bias)
evidence.effect: Radiologists changed assessment from positive to negative in 21 to 41% of exams even though this was incorrect in 31 to 38% of cases.
evidence.quote: In our study, radiologists changed their assessment from positive to negative in 21 to 41% of the exams even though this was incorrect in 31 to 38% of cases.

evidence.title: Heterogeneity and predictors of the effects of AI assistance on radiologists
evidence.outcome: Effect of incorrect AI predictions on radiologist performance (automation bias/overreliance)
evidence.effect: Inaccurate AI predictions adversely affected radiologist performance on the aggregate of all pathologies and on half of the individual pathologies investigated.
evidence.quote: Instead, we found that the occurrence of AI errors strongly influences treatment outcomes, with inaccurate AI predictions adversely affecting radiologist performance on the aggregate of all pathologies and on half of the individual pathologies investigated.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted full-mouth radiograph mounting in dental education
evidence.outcome: Whether students corrected errors in AI-pre-mounted radiographs
evidence.effect: Students reviewing AI pre-mounted radiographs had decreased accuracy compared with manual mounting (p < 0.01), suggesting incorrect AI outputs were not always detected or corrected.
evidence.quote: Students with AI presented with a decreased accuracy in FMS radiograph mounting.

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence Efficacy as a Function of Trainee Interpreter Proficiency: Lessons from a Randomized Controlled Trial
evidence.outcome: Whether trainees detected and overruled incorrect AI outputs
evidence.effect: Both groups considerably less accurate with incorrect AI results; medical students less likely than residents to overrule incorrect AI interpretations and less accurate with aid than AI alone.
evidence.quote: However, medical students were less likely than resident trainees to overrule incorrect artificial intelligence interpretations and were less accurate, even with diagnostic aid, than the artificial intelligence was by itself.

evidence.title: The clinical value of artificial intelligence in assisting junior radiologists in thyroid ultrasound: a multicenter prospective study from real clinical practice
evidence.outcome: Junior radiologists misled by incorrect AI outputs
evidence.effect: AI output reverted 31 originally correct junior classifications (17 benign, 14 malignant), versus 193 corrected misclassifications.
evidence.quote: In total, there were substantially more cases where the junior radiologists benefited from consulting diagnostic results by the AI system than being misled (193 vs 31 summing up benign and malignant classified nodules).

evidence.title: Reporting radiographers' interaction with Artificial Intelligence-How do different forms of AI feedback impact trust and decision switching?
evidence.outcome: decision switching after AI feedback
evidence.effect: 2/216 (1.1%) would change; 35/216 (15.7%) might; 179/216 (83.5%) would retain initial decision.
evidence.quote: Of the total 216 responses to this question across all datasets there were only two instances (examination 11b and 1c) where participants indicated that they would change their mind in response to the AI feedback (1.1%), n = 35 (15.7%) indicated that they might change their mind from their initial diagnosis and the remainder (n = 179, 83.5%) indicated that they would retain their initial decision.

evidence.title: Comparison of AI-integrated pathways with human-AI interaction in population mammographic screening for breast cancer
evidence.outcome: Effect of simulated automation bias (readers agreeing with incorrect AI) on system sensitivity/specificity
evidence.effect: Negative interaction in AI triage dropped sensitivity by 5.6 points to about 73.1% and specificity to 93.5%; single-reader negative interaction lowered sensitivity/specificity to ~62.6% and 93.9%.
evidence.quote: The sensitivity can quickly drop by 5.6 percentage points to about 73.1% (6.7 percentage points lower than the baseline standard of care) and the specificity can drop to 93.5% when human readers follow the mistakes made by the AI reader.

evidence.title: Automation Bias in AI-Decision Support: Results from an Empirical Study
evidence.venue: Studies in health technology and informatics
evidence.outcome: Agreement rate with wrong AI recommendations (automation bias) and factors associated with it
evidence.effect: Automation bias occurred and was associated with user factors. Diagnostic performance, wound care training, physician profession and female gender reduced false agreement. Higher perceived system benefit increased it. Non-specialists were most susceptible.
evidence.quote: This study highlights that non-specialists, who stand to gain the most from CDSS, are also the most susceptible to automation bias, emphasizing the need for specialized training to mitigate this risk and ensure diagnostic accuracy and patient safety.

evidence.title: "Doctor ChatGPT, Can You Help Me?" The Patient's Perspective: Cross-Sectional Study
evidence.outcome: Whether users detect incorrect or harmful AI outputs
evidence.effect: Specialists rated potentially harmful ChatGPT responses lower on usefulness (3.93 vs 4.59) and correctness (4.62 vs 3.84), P<.001; patients showed no such difference.
evidence.quote: Alarmingly, patients are not able to independently recognize these potential dangers.

evidence.title: OSAIRIS: Lessons Learned From the Hospital-Based Implementation and Evaluation of an Open-Source Deep-Learning Model for Radiotherapy Image Segmentation
evidence.venue: Clinical oncology (Royal College of Radiologists (Great Britain))
evidence.outcome: anchoring bias in editing
evidence.effect: Anchoring bias was present when clinicians edited AI-generated contours, more pronounced for some structures.
evidence.quote: Our safety and risk-mitigation exercise showed that anchoring bias is present when clinicians edit AI-generated contours, with the effect seemingly more pronounced for some structures over others.

evidence.title: Facilitating Trust Calibration in Artificial Intelligence-Driven Diagnostic Decision Support Systems for Determining Physicians' Diagnostic Accuracy: Quasi-Experimental Study
evidence.outcome: Whether physicians detect incorrect AI outputs (trust calibration correctness) and overconfidence in AI
evidence.effect: Trust calibration correct in 61.5% (123/200); accuracy 54.5% when correct vs 20.8% when incorrect; intervention group estimated AI accuracy ~30% higher than actual.
evidence.quote: The secondary outcome, the correctness of trust calibration in the intervention group, was 61.5% (123/200; Table 2 ).

evidence.title: What makes a 'good' decision with artificial intelligence? A grounded theory study in paediatric care
evidence.outcome: Automation bias when model explanation conflicted with clinician prior knowledge
evidence.effect: Many participants assumed their own judgement was incorrect when the model's explanation conflicted with it; others rejected the incorrect explanation using their medical knowledge.
evidence.quote: We found evidence of automation bias, with many participants assuming that if the model's explanation conflicted with their prior knowledge that their judgement was incorrect; others concluded the exact opposite, drawing from their medical knowledge base to reject the incorrect information provided in the explanation.

evidence.title: Safety of human-AI cooperative decision-making within intensive care: A physical simulation study
evidence.outcome: detection of unsafe AI outputs
evidence.effect: Unsafe recommendations stopped 83 ± 4% versus safe 29 ± 4%; stopped/escalated unsafe recommendations rose to 92 ± 3%.
evidence.quote: In total, unsafe AI recommendations were stopped more often than safe AI recommendations (83 ± 4%, 95% CI: 0.75–0.91 vs. 29 ± 4%, 95% CI: 0.21–0.37, p < 0.0001).

evidence.title: Integrating AI into clinical education: evaluating general practice trainees' proficiency in distinguishing AI-generated hallucinations and impacting factors
evidence.outcome: Users' ability to detect incorrect AI outputs (hallucinations) from ChatGPT-4o
evidence.effect: GP trainees detected hallucinations with 55.0% mean accuracy and d' of 0.39; the authors conclude they faced challenges identifying errors, particularly in clinical scenarios.
evidence.quote: The study concluded that GP trainees faced challenges in identifying ChatGPT-4o's errors, particularly in clinical scenarios.

evidence.title: Psychological Factors Influencing Appropriate Reliance on AI-enabled Clinical Decision Support Systems: Experimental Web-Based Study Among Dermatologists
evidence.outcome: Reliance on correct versus incorrect AI advice; relative AI reliance and self-reliance among dermatologists
evidence.effect: Reliance stronger for correct than incorrect advice (t222=4.2; P<.001); mean relative AI reliance 10.04% and relative self-reliance 85.6%, i.e., high self-reliance, low AI reliance; accuracy improved only 1% with AI.
evidence.quote: Reliance on AI was stronger for correct advice than for incorrect advice (t<sub>222</sub>=4.2; P<.001; Cohen d=0.1).

evidence.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Models in Clinical Infectious Disease Consultations: A Cross-Sectional Analysis Among Specialists and Resident Trainees
evidence.outcome: Human vulnerability to failing to detect incorrect or harmful AI outputs
evidence.effect: Specialists rated responses higher than resident trainees in all domains (p < 0.001) and were five times more likely to consider responses harmless, indicating vulnerabilities in safeguarding against harmful outputs.
evidence.quote: In our analysis, we have demonstrated disconcerting human vulnerabilities in safeguarding against potentially harmful outputs, which seemed to be most apparent among experienced specialists.

evidence.title: Opportunities and risks of artificial intelligence in patient portal messaging in primary care
evidence.outcome: Whether physicians detected incorrect AI outputs (automation bias/overreliance)
evidence.effect: Physicians missed 65-75% of erroneous drafts (13-15 of 20); 90% agreed they trusted the AI tool and 75% believed drafts were safe to use.
evidence.quote: Participants missed an average of 2.67 out of four (66.6%) erroneous AI drafts.

evidence.title: The impact of AI feedback on the accuracy of diagnosis, decision switching and trust in radiography
evidence.outcome: automation bias after incorrect AI feedback
evidence.effect: Incorrect AI feedback reduced accuracy by 4.8% overall, 9.6% in students and 4.3% in radiographers.
evidence.quote: A greater impact was seen in the student group where accuracy fell by 9.6% compared with 4.3% amongst radiographers, suggesting in this sample that the student group is more susceptible to automation bias ( Table 5b ).

evidence.title: Translating the machine; An assessment of clinician understanding of ophthalmological artificial intelligence outputs
evidence.outcome: overreliance on incorrect AI outputs
evidence.effect: With complex incorrect AI outcomes, experienced clinicians correctly reduced trust; less experienced clinicians gave mixed feedback.
evidence.quote: When clinical scenarios were complex with incorrect AI outcomes, a mixed response to explainability led to correctly reduced trust in experienced clinicians but mixed feedback amongst less experienced clinicians.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence algorithm improves radiologists' bone age assessment accuracy
evidence.venue: Journal of the Chinese Medical Association : JCMA
evidence.outcome: Automation bias and AI disagreements by experience
evidence.effect: Worsened ≥1 y: 28 (2.3%) vs improved ≥1 y: 201 (16.8%); disagreements: S1/S2 65/65, M1/M2 23/55, J1/J2 18/27.
evidence.quote: Radiologists reading BAs were prone to automation bias when being supported by an AI algorithm, especially in less experienced radiologists.

evidence.title: Enhancing the Accuracy of Human Phenotype Ontology Identification: Comparative Evaluation of Multimodal Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: Whether physicians detected or were misled by incorrect AI outputs (anchoring)
evidence.effect: For Bardet-Biedl syndrome, MLLM missed 'polydactyly'; error rate was higher in MLLM-assisted group (6/10) than manual (4/10), though overall accuracy improved.
evidence.quote: This led to a higher error rate in the MLLM-assisted group (6/10 physicians) compared to the manual group (4/10).
evidence.sample_unit: junior physicians (27 patient images each, 540 descriptions)

evidence.title: Empirically derived evaluation requirements for responsible deployments of AI in safety-critical settings

commentary.bottom_line: Four simulation or replay studies show that pre-deployment tests of whether clinicians catch incorrect AI outputs can be run and produce usable detection rates, but none tests whether doing such an assessment reduces harm after deployment. Certainty for the practice itself is very low, while 82 hazard studies document that users sometimes accept incorrect outputs.

perspectives.view: All four tests are level 4 offline studies in single countries, covering 38 intensivists, 99 biopsies, 1142 reader-case pairs, and 86 OCT scans. Three support the practice and one is mixed. They measure detection during the assessment, not the effect of assessing on later patient outcomes, so indirectness and imprecision lower certainty to very low.

In one replay study, surgeons rejected 9 of 13 AI false positives, yet 4 errors were still confirmed. Hazard studies show accuracy falling from 84.9% to 73.3% with flawed LLM advice, and resistance to incorrect answers falling from 92% to 34.8% when citations appeared. Assessments that inject known errors may reveal these failure modes before patients are exposed.

Detection varies with user experience. In one simulation, trainees reached 0% accuracy when the AI was wrong versus 66.67% for trained clinicians, and confidence stayed high regardless. Readers were persuaded by correct AI output in only 30% to 45% of cases, which suggests assessments may need to measure algorithm aversion as well as overreliance across the intended users.

None of the four tests reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy participants. One trial in China that enrolled non-English-speaking, low-literacy, low-income, and rural patients found no direct adoption of LLM content in notes (F1 0.57), but that trial examines the hazard and does not test the assessment practice.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software describes overreliance arising from information gaps, and the CHAI and FUTURE-AI frameworks call for evaluating automation bias and uncertainty aversion during usability testing. These sources recommend assessment without citing a trial showing that pre-deployment assessment changes outcomes, so the recommendation rests on consensus.

The tests used small rater panels, such as 5 neurosurgeons scoring 86 scans and 38 intensivists in simulation, which suggests a pre-deployment detection study can be run with modest staffing. None of the studies reported cost, staff time, or how often the assessment should be repeated after model updates.

In the intensivist simulation, many clinicians who rejected unsafe recommendations sought senior assistance, while a few accepted them after nurse influence. In Kenya, a minority of frontline workers reported deferring diagnosis to the AI. These findings suggest assessments may need to examine team dynamics and escalation paths, because patients depend on a person who questions the output.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares deployments that underwent a pre-deployment assessment of automation bias with deployments that did not, and none follows whether detection rates measured in simulation predict acceptance of AI errors in live care. Prospective studies with patient outcomes, across settings and levels of user experience, would address this gap.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the four tests of the practice included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and all were offline studies with clinician raters in the United Kingdom, Norway, the United States, and Russia. Detection rates from these settings may not transfer to under-resourced sites where staffing, training, and time pressure differ.
